title: 36 In vitro assessment of the neuroactive potential of the rumen microbiome
content:
Abstract
The gut-brain axis, a bidirectional communication network linking the central and enteric nervous systems is crucial for regulating stress responses, metabolism, immune system, and cognitive functions in animals. The gut microbiota is actively involved in this crosstalk, partly through bacteria-derived neuroactive compounds, such as neurotransmitters and their precursors. However, the neuroactive potential of rumen microbiota in ruminants remains largely unexplored. This study aimed to investigate whether rumen microbiota can synthesize neuroactive compounds and to identify their potential microbial producers. Three rumen fluid samples from cannulated beef cattle were cultured anaerobically in glass fleakers at 39 ℃ in a warm shaker bath for 48 hours. Samples (2 mL) were taken at 0 h, 4 h, 12 h, 24 h, and 48 h for neurotransmitter and microbiota profiling. The concentrations of neurotransmitters and their precursors were quantified via liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) and bacterial composition was analyzed using the full-length 16S rRNA sequencing. Temporal changes in neuroactive compound concentrations were assessed using one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post-hoc test, and Pearson correlation was analyzed between neuroactive compound concentrations and bacterial relative abundances. LC-MS detected the presence of neurotransmitters acetylcholine, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), glutamate, and precursors 3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetic acid, tryptophan, and tryptamine A in the rumen fluid samples. GABA, the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter, exhibited a gradual increase in concentration from 0 h (425.7 ± 101.6 ng/mL) to 24 h (1097.1 ± 80.3 ng/mL) during in vitro culture (P = 0.07), followed by a decline at 48 h (443.6 ± 225.1 ng/mL, P = 0.079). A similar pattern was observed for glutamate, the main excitatory neurotransmitter (0 h: 38.3 ± 18.8 μg/mL; 24 h: 34.3 ± 10.8 μg/mL; 48 h: 33.9 ± 9.1 μg/mL), although not significant (P = 0.83). The observed increase in neurotransmitter concentrations during the first 24 hours suggests that rumen microbes can synthesize these compounds in addition to host cells, with the subsequent reduction potentially due to decreased bacterial viability over time. Pearson correlation analysis revealed several bacterial species that were significantly associated with neurotransmitter concentrations. For instance, Helcococcus sueciensis (Rp = 0.678, P = 0.005), Proteiniclasticum ruminis (Rp = 0.675, P = 0.006), and Clostridium sulfidigenes (Rp = 0.649, P = 0.009) showed positive correlations with GABA levels, while Odoribacter splanchnicus (Rp = 0.650, P = 0.009), Howardella ureilytica (Rp = 0.609, P = 0.016), and Lactobacillus paracasei (Rp = 0.597, P = 0.019) showed positive correlations with glutamate concentrations. These findings suggest that certain rumen bacterial species possess the capacity to synthesize specific neurotransmitters. However, further research warranted exploration of the rumen-microbiome-brain axis to confirm the capability of the identified species to produce neuroactive compounds and the regulatory effects of rumen microbial-derived neurotransmitters on nervous system of ruminants.
